title: Semi-voiced H ゜— パ ピ プ ペ ポ

points.shortDescription: The small circle that creates P sounds from the H-row
points.explanation: Just as in hiragana, the handakuten (゜) — the small circle placed at the top-right of H-row katakana — transforms them into P sounds. ハ→パ, ヒ→ピ, フ→プ, ヘ→ペ, ホ→ポ. The P-row katakana are extremely common in loanwords from English and other European languages, since 'p' sounds are abundant in those languages. You'll encounter P-row characters constantly in katakana reading: パン (bread), ピアノ (piano), プール (pool), ペン (pen), and ポスター (poster) are just the beginning.
rules: Handakuten (゜) = small circle top-right = H-row becomes P-row.
ハ→パ, ヒ→ピ, フ→プ, ヘ→ペ, ホ→ポ — applies only to the H-row.
P-row is extremely common in katakana because English has many 'p' sounds.
points.flashcardAnswer: handakuten — small circle converts H-row to P-row (パピプペポ)

points.name: パ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぱ — 'pa'; handakuten version of ハ
points.explanation: パ makes the same 'pa' sound as hiragana ぱ — unaspirated 'p' before 'ah'. It's ハ plus the handakuten circle. パ appears in some of the most common katakana words: パン (bread — still from Portuguese 'pão'), パーティー (party), パスポート (passport), and パソコン (personal computer — a Japanese coinage from 'personal computer'). パソコン is a perfect example of Japan's creative word-shortening: 'personal' + 'computer' → パーソナルコンピューター → パソコン. This type of shortening is extremely common.
rules: パ = ハ + handakuten; unaspirated 'p' before 'ah'.
パソコン (personal computer) = パーソナル (personal) + コンピューター (computer) → abbreviated to パソコン.
Japanese frequently abbreviates long katakana words: パソコン, スマホ, コンビニ, etc.
points.flashcardAnswer: pa — handakuten version of ハ; like 'pa' in 'party'

points.name: ピ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぴ — 'pi'; handakuten version of ヒ
points.explanation: ピ makes the same 'pi' sound as hiragana ぴ — unaspirated 'p' before bright 'ee'. It's ヒ plus the handakuten. ピ appears in ピアノ (piano), ピザ (pizza), ピンク (pink), and ピーマン (green pepper — from French 'piment'). ピアノ is iconic — Japan has an extremely strong piano culture, with many children learning piano from a young age. ピーマン is another French-origin word (like ズボン) from the Meiji era. Japan's vocabulary is a fascinating collage of historical borrowing from Portuguese, Dutch, German, French, English, and Chinese.
rules: ピ = ヒ + handakuten; unaspirated 'p' before 'ee'.
ピアノ (piano) is culturally significant — Japan has one of the world's highest piano lesson participation rates.
ピーマン (green bell pepper) is from French 'piment' — another Meiji-era French borrowing.
points.flashcardAnswer: pi — handakuten version of ヒ; like 'pi' in 'piano'

points.name: プ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぷ — 'pu'; handakuten version of フ
points.explanation: プ makes the same 'pu' sound as hiragana ぷ — unaspirated 'p' before the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'. It's フ plus the handakuten, transforming the bilabial fricative into a bilabial stop. プ appears in プール (pool), プリン (pudding / flan — a hugely popular convenience store dessert in Japan), プレゼント (present / gift), and プロ (professional). プリン (from English 'pudding' via French 'pudding') refers specifically to the caramel-topped egg custard dessert found in every Japanese convenience store. It's become a beloved cultural icon.
rules: プ = フ + handakuten; bilabial fricative 'f' becomes bilabial stop 'p'.
プリン (pudding = Japanese caramel custard) is one of Japan's most beloved convenience store desserts.
プレゼント (present/gift) is one of the most socially important words — Japan has elaborate gifting culture.
points.flashcardAnswer: pu — handakuten version of フ; like 'pu' in 'pool'

points.name: ペ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぺ — 'pe'; handakuten version of ヘ
points.explanation: ペ makes the same 'pe' sound as hiragana ぺ — unaspirated 'p' before 'eh'. It's ヘ plus the handakuten. Since ヘ and へ are nearly identical visually, ペ and ぺ are also close pairs. ペ appears in ペン (pen), ペット (pet), ページ (page), and ペットボトル (plastic bottle — literally 'PET bottle', from the plastic material PET/polyethylene terephthalate). ペットボトル is widely used in Japan because plastic bottles are ubiquitous, and the word is used on recycling bins and in everyday conversation about recycling.
rules: ペ = ヘ + handakuten; since ヘ ≈ へ, ペ ≈ ぺ visually.
ペン (pen) and ペット (pet) are among the most common everyday ペ words.
ペットボトル (plastic bottle) is important vocabulary for Japan's recycling culture.
points.flashcardAnswer: pe — handakuten version of ヘ; like 'pe' in 'pep'

points.name: ポ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぽ — 'po'; handakuten version of ホ
points.explanation: ポ makes the same 'po' sound as hiragana ぽ — unaspirated 'p' before 'oh'. It's ホ plus the handakuten. ポ appears in ポスター (poster), ポテト (potato — especially French fries, as in マクドナルドのポテト = McDonald's fries), ポケット (pocket), and ポイント (point — including loyalty points, which are huge in Japan's retail culture). Japan's ポイントシステム (point/loyalty system) is extraordinarily developed — nearly every store has a point card, and collecting ポイント is a regular part of daily shopping.
rules: ポ = ホ + handakuten; 'h' becomes 'p' before 'oh'.
ポテト in Japan often specifically means French fries, not raw potato (which is じゃがいも).
ポイント (points/loyalty points) is central to Japan's retail culture — every store wants you to join their ポイントカード.
points.flashcardAnswer: po — handakuten version of ホ; like 'po' in 'post'

chapterPractice.prompt: The P-row (パピプペポ) uses the handakuten ゜. Which row does it transform?
chapterPractice.explanation: The handakuten ゜ only applies to the H-row: ハ→パ, ヒ→ピ, フ→プ, ヘ→ペ, ホ→ポ. No other katakana row has a handakuten form. The P-row is important because English loanwords frequently contain 'p' sounds.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana matches the katakana ピ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ピ and ぴ both make the 'pi' sound. Katakana ピ is ヒ (hi) with a handakuten; hiragana ぴ is ひ (hi) with a handakuten. Same logic, both scripts.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: プレゼント (purezento) means 'present' or 'gift'. プ (pu) + レ (re) + ゼ (ze) + ン (n) + ト (to) = purezento. Japan has an elaborate gift-giving culture — プレゼントをあげる (to give a gift) and プレゼントをもらう (to receive a gift) are essential vocabulary.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ポイント (pointo) means 'point' — including the loyalty reward points that are a cornerstone of Japanese retail culture. ポ (po) + イ (i) + ン (n) + ト (to) = pointo. Congratulations — you've now completed all of the katakana characters!
